title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself: your name, where you are from, where you live and which languages you speak.
intro:
In this unit you meet the personal pronouns and the verb 'to be' — ਹਾਂ, ਹੈਂ, ਹੈ, ਹੋ, ਹਨ — which ends a huge number of Punjabi sentences. You will also learn the main question words, so you can ask people about themselves.

Notice that ਇਹ (*é*) 'this/he/she' and ਉਹ (*ó*) 'that/he/she' are pronounced as a single vowel with high tone: the written ਹ is not heard.

vocab.note: pronounced with high tone, no h
the past of 'to be' for all persons in speech
comes after the word it modifies

phrases.en: Where do you live? (to a man / polite)

grammar.title: Pronouns and the verb 'to be'
grammar.body:
The present tense of 'to be' changes with the subject:

ਮੈਂ ਹਾਂ — I am
ਅਸੀਂ ਹਾਂ — we are
ਤੂੰ ਹੈਂ — you are (intimate)
ਤੁਸੀਂ ਹੋ — you are (polite/plural)
ਇਹ / ਉਹ ਹੈ — he/she/it/this/that is
ਇਹ / ਉਹ ਹਨ — they/these/those are (spoken Majhi often uses ਨੇ: ਉਹ ਘਰ ਨੇ)

Punjabi has **no separate words for he and she**: ਇਹ is someone near, ਉਹ someone further away or not present. Gender shows up in verbs and adjectives instead. ਇਹ and ਉਹ are also used for one respected person with plural verb (ਉਹ ਸਾਡੇ ਅਧਿਆਪਕ ਹਨ).

The past 'was/were' is simply **ਸੀ** for every person in everyday speech (formal writing has ਸਾਂ, ਸੈਂ, ਸਨ).

examples.en: They are from Canada. / He is from Canada (respectful).

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.body:
Question words stay in the position of the answer — usually right before the verb:

ਕੀ — what · ਕੌਣ — who · ਕਿੱਥੇ — where · ਕਿੱਥੋਂ — from where · ਕਦੋਂ — when · ਕਿਉਂ — why · ਕਿਵੇਂ — how

Note the pattern: ਕਿੱਥੇ 'where' + ਤੋਂ 'from' gives ਕਿੱਥੋਂ 'from where'. ਕੀ at the very start of a sentence is not 'what' but simply marks a yes/no question.

examples.en: Why are you learning (do you learn) Punjabi?

dialogue.title: At the gurdwara langar
dialogue.setting: Tom, a learner from London, sits next to Harpreet while eating in the community kitchen.

lines.speaker: Harpreet
lines.native: ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ ਜੀ। ਤੁਹਾਡਾ ਨਾਂ ਕੀ ਹੈ?
lines.roman: sat srī akāl jī. tuā́ḍā nāṃ kī hai?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: My name is Tom. And yours?

lines.speaker: Harpreet
lines.native: ਮੈਂ ਹਰਪ੍ਰੀਤ ਹਾਂ। ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿੱਥੋਂ ਹੋ?
lines.roman: maiṃ Harprīt hāṃ. tusīṃ kitthoṃ ho?
lines.en: I'm Harpreet. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: ਥੋੜ੍ਹੀ ਥੋੜ੍ਹੀ। ਮੈਂ ਸਿੱਖ ਰਿਹਾ ਹਾਂ।
lines.roman: thóṛī thóṛī. maiṃ sikkh ríā hāṃ.

lines.speaker: Harpreet
lines.native: ਬਹੁਤ ਵਧੀਆ! ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿੱਥੇ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ ਹੋ?
lines.roman: báut vádīā! tusīṃ kitthe rénde ho?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: ਮੈਂ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ ਰਹਿੰਦਾ ਹਾਂ, ਇੱਕ ਹੋਟਲ ਵਿੱਚ।
lines.roman: maiṃ Amritsar réndā hāṃ, ikk hoṭal vich.
lines.en: I'm staying in Amritsar, in a hotel.

lines.speaker: Harpreet
lines.native: ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਮਿਲ ਕੇ ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ ਹੋਈ, ਟੌਮ ਜੀ।
lines.roman: tuā́nūṃ mil ke xushī hoī, Ṭaum jī.

culture: Asking where someone is from (ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿੱਥੋਂ ਹੋ?) is a friendly opener in Punjab, and people often mean their ancestral village or district, not just their current city. Around a third of Punjabi speakers in India and Pakistan have relatives abroad, so ਵਲੈਤ (*valait*, 'abroad', originally Britain), Canada and Australia come up quickly in conversation. At a gurdwara anyone, of any faith, may eat at the free community kitchen (ਲੰਗਰ, *langar*) — cover your head and remove your shoes.
